concepts.name: MIGA's Establishment and Institutional Identity within the World Bank Group
key_dimensions: Year of establishment (1988) and founding convention — Seoul Convention 1985
MIGA as one of five institutions of the World Bank Group — distinction from IBRD, IDA, IFC, ICSID
UPSC trap: MIGA vs IFC — both deal with private sector but different mandates (guarantee vs lending)
Headquarters in Washington D.C. and membership-based structure

concepts.name: Core Mandate and Objective of MIGA
key_dimensions: Promoting foreign direct investment (FDI) into developing countries through political risk insurance
Distinction from development lending — MIGA does not lend money, it provides guarantees
Focus on encouraging private sector investment where commercial insurers may not operate
UPSC trap: MIGA's mandate is 'guarantee' not 'investment' — often confused with IFC which actually invests

concepts.name: Political Risk Insurance (PRI) — The Primary Instrument of MIGA
key_dimensions: Definition: Insurance against non-commercial risks arising from host government actions or political instability
Difference between political risk and commercial/credit risk — MIGA covers only the former
Why PRI is critical for developing-country investments: sovereign unpredictability, weak institutions
UPSC trap: MIGA does NOT cover commercial risks like market fluctuations or business failure

concepts.name: Four Classic Categories of Political Risk Covered by MIGA
key_dimensions: Transfer Restriction: inability to convert or transfer local currency profits abroad
Expropriation: direct or creeping nationalization of assets by host government
War, Civil Disturbance, and Civil War: physical damage or business interruption due to conflict
Breach of Contract: host government's failure to honor contractual obligations (arbitration clause trigger)

concepts.name: Non-Honoring of Sovereign Financial Obligations — MIGA's Expanded Coverage
key_dimensions: Covers situations where a sovereign or sub-sovereign entity fails to make payment on a financial obligation
Added to address gaps in traditional PRI — relevant for PPP projects and infrastructure bonds
Difference from 'Breach of Contract' — non-honoring is specifically financial, breach is broader contractual
UPSC angle: Demonstrates MIGA's evolution beyond the original four risks

concepts.name: Eligible Investors and Host Countries under MIGA
key_dimensions: Investors must be nationals of a MIGA member country other than the host country
Investment must flow from a member country INTO a developing member country
Eligible investments: equity, loans, technical assistance, management contracts, and certain shareholder loans
UPSC trap: A domestic investor cannot use MIGA to cover investments in their own country

concepts.name: MIGA's Membership Structure and Voting Rights
key_dimensions: Membership open to all World Bank (IBRD) members — two categories: Category One (developed) and Category Two (developing)
Voting rights based on subscribed shares — larger shareholders have more votes
India's membership and its classification as a developing/Category Two member
UPSC trap: MIGA membership is not automatic with UN membership — must separately join IBRD first

concepts.name: MIGA's Governance Structure — Council of Governors and Board of Directors
key_dimensions: Council of Governors: highest authority, one governor per member country (typically Finance Minister or Central Bank Governor)
Board of Directors: 25 directors, responsible for day-to-day operations and policy decisions
President of the World Bank Group serves as ex-officio Chairperson of the Board
UPSC trap: Governance structure mirrors World Bank but MIGA has its own separate legal personality

concepts.name: MIGA vs. IFC — Structural and Functional Comparison
key_dimensions: IFC provides loans and equity investments; MIGA provides guarantees and insurance — no direct financing
Both target private sector in developing countries but through fundamentally different instruments
IFC focuses on commercial viability; MIGA focuses on de-risking political/non-commercial environment
UPSC trap: Both are part of WBG but IFC is much larger in financial exposure; MIGA's exposure is contingent liability

concepts.name: MIGA vs. ICSID — Role in Investment Dispute Resolution
key_dimensions: ICSID (International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes) handles arbitration of investor-state disputes
MIGA does not resolve disputes — it indemnifies investors and then pursues subrogation against the host state
Subrogation: After paying a claim, MIGA steps into the shoes of the investor to recover from the host government
UPSC trap: MIGA and ICSID are both WBG institutions but serve entirely different functions in the investment protection ecosystem

concepts.name: Subrogation Rights of MIGA — Post-Claim Mechanism
key_dimensions: After compensating an investor, MIGA acquires the investor's rights against the host country
MIGA then negotiates with the host government for reimbursement — leveraging its multilateral status
This acts as a deterrent for host governments to violate investor rights (reputational and financial consequences)
UPSC angle: Subrogation transforms MIGA from passive insurer to active enforcer of investment protections

concepts.name: MIGA's Role in Conflict-Affected and Fragile States
key_dimensions: MIGA has a specific mandate to support investment in IDA-eligible and fragile/conflict-affected states (FCS)
War and civil disturbance coverage is particularly critical for these economies
MIGA's presence signals multilateral backing, crowding in private investment where others fear to tread
Examples: MIGA guarantees in Sub-Saharan Africa, post-conflict reconstruction contexts

concepts.name: MIGA and Climate Finance / Green Investment Guarantees
key_dimensions: MIGA increasingly used to de-risk renewable energy and climate-resilient infrastructure investments
Aligns with World Bank Group's climate commitments and Paris Agreement targets
Political risk is a major barrier to green investment in developing countries — MIGA addresses this gap
UPSC current affairs angle: MIGA's role in mobilizing private climate finance for developing nations

concepts.name: MIGA's Financial Structure — Callable Capital and Contingent Liability
key_dimensions: MIGA's balance sheet consists largely of contingent liabilities (guarantees issued, not loans disbursed)
Funded by subscribed capital from member countries — both paid-in and callable portions
Gross exposure vs. net exposure — MIGA can reinsure with private insurers to manage risk
UPSC trap: Unlike IBRD/IDA, MIGA does not raise money from bond markets — its instrument is the guarantee, not debt

concepts.name: MIGA's Cooperation with National Export Credit Agencies (ECAs)
key_dimensions: ECAs (like EXIM Bank, ECGC in India) provide export credit and investment insurance at bilateral level
MIGA operates at multilateral level — covers investments from any member country into developing countries
Co-insurance and reinsurance arrangements between MIGA and national ECAs are common
UPSC trap: ECGC covers export credit risk; MIGA covers political risk on FDI — different instruments for different risks

concepts.name: India's Engagement with MIGA — FDI Implications
key_dimensions: India is both a member country and a host country for MIGA-backed investments
MIGA guarantees can facilitate inward FDI into India by reducing political risk perceptions of foreign investors
Indian investors investing abroad (especially in Africa, South Asia) can also use MIGA coverage
UPSC angle: India's status as a developing member means it benefits from MIGA's mandate on both inward and outward investment

concepts.name: The Seoul Convention 1985 — Legal Foundation of MIGA
key_dimensions: Formally adopted at Seoul in 1985, entered into force in 1988 — created MIGA as a treaty-based organization
Established the legal framework for political risk insurance at the multilateral level
Distinction: Seoul Convention governs MIGA; Washington Convention 1965 governs ICSID
UPSC trap: Often confused — Seoul (MIGA, 1985/88) vs Washington (ICSID, 1965) vs Bretton Woods (IBRD/IMF, 1944)

concepts.name: MIGA's Role in Crowding-In Private Investment (Additionality Principle)
key_dimensions: MIGA focuses on 'additionality' — supporting investments that would NOT happen without its guarantee
By absorbing political risk, MIGA unlocks private capital that commercial insurers would reject
Measured by: total investment mobilized per dollar of guarantee issued (leverage ratio)
UPSC angle: Relevant to discussions on blended finance, private sector mobilization for SDGs

concepts.name: MIGA's Environmental and Social Standards in Project Approval
key_dimensions: MIGA applies the World Bank Group's Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) to guaranteed projects
Projects must comply with IFC Performance Standards — covering labor, indigenous peoples, biodiversity
MIGA can deny or withdraw guarantees for projects that violate E&S standards
UPSC angle: MIGA as a tool of conditionality — not just financial protection but governance standard-setter

concepts.name: Distinction Between MIGA Guarantees and Bilateral Investment Treaties (BITs)
key_dimensions: BITs are state-to-state agreements providing legal protections to investors; MIGA is a multilateral insurance mechanism
BITs rely on investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS); MIGA compensates and then exercises subrogation
MIGA guarantee is faster and more certain than BIT-based arbitration (which can take years)
UPSC trap: Both MIGA and BITs protect against expropriation, but through entirely different legal and financial mechanisms
